meta_title: NCERT Class 12 Maths Solutions: Integration Ex 7.8
meta_desc: Step-by-step NCERT Class 12 Maths solutions for Integration Exercise 7.8 — the definite integral as the limit of a sum, with a free 8-question quiz.

quiz.title: Definite Integral as the Limit of a Sum Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on evaluating definite integrals from first principles — the limit-of-a-sum definition used throughout Exercise 7.8. Answer each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Definite integral as the limit of a sum (Class 12, Exercise 7.8)

questions.q: In the limit-of-a-sum definition of ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f(x) dx, the width h of each of the n subintervals is:
questions.explanation: The interval [a, b] is split into n equal parts, so each strip has width h = (b − a)/n. As n → ∞, h → 0.

questions.q: As the number of subintervals n → ∞, the quantity nh in this definition tends to:
questions.explanation: Since h = (b − a)/n, the product nh = b − a for every n, so it stays fixed at b − a as n → ∞.

questions.q: The definite integral as a limit of a sum is written ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f(x) dx = lim<sub>n→∞</sub> h [f(a) + f(a+h) + ... + f(a+(n−1)h)]. The sum inside has how many terms?
questions.explanation: The terms run from f(a) to f(a+(n−1)h), i.e. f(a+rh) for r = 0, 1, ..., n−1 — exactly n terms, one per subinterval.

questions.q: Using the limit of a sum, ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> x dx equals:
questions.explanation: Here a = 0, b = 2, so h = 2/n and f(a+rh) = rh. The sum h∑rh = h²·n(n−1)/2 = (4/n²)·n(n−1)/2 → 2. (Check: ½×2² = 2.)

questions.q: Which standard result is needed to evaluate ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> x² dx by the limit of a sum?
options: Sum of a GP with ratio e<sup>h</sup>
questions.explanation: The sum ∑(a+rh)² expands to a term in ∑r², so the formula for the sum of squares of the first (n−1) natural numbers is required.

questions.q: Evaluating ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> e<sup>x</sup> dx as a limit of a sum gives a geometric series. Its value is:
questions.explanation: The terms f(rh) = e<sup>rh</sup> form a GP with common ratio e<sup>h</sup>. Summing and taking n → ∞ (using (e<sup>h</sup>−1)/h → 1) gives e<sup>1</sup> − e<sup>0</sup> = e − 1.

questions.q: By the limit of a sum, ∫<sub>1</sub><sup>3</sup> (2x + 1) dx equals:
questions.explanation: The antiderivative check: x² + x from 1 to 3 = (9+3) − (1+1) = 12 − 2 = 10, which matches the limit-of-a-sum value.

questions.q: In the limit-of-a-sum definition, the sample point f(a + rh) is taken at the:
questions.explanation: The NCERT form uses r = 0, 1, ..., n−1, so the heights are read at the left endpoints a, a+h, a+2h, ... . As n → ∞ the choice of endpoint does not change the limit.

faq.q: What does Exercise 7.8 of Class 12 Maths cover?
faq.a: Exercise 7.8 asks you to evaluate definite integrals as the limit of a sum — the first-principles definition — rather than using antiderivatives. You split [a, b] into n equal strips of width h = (b − a)/n, add the areas, and take the limit as n → ∞.

faq.q: What is the formula for a definite integral as a limit of a sum?
faq.a: ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> f(x) dx = lim<sub>n→∞</sub> h [f(a) + f(a+h) + f(a+2h) + ... + f(a+(n−1)h)], where h = (b − a)/n. It is the sum of n thin rectangles whose heights are taken at the left endpoints.

faq.q: Which summation formulas should I memorise for this exercise?
faq.a: Keep three ready: the sum of the first (n−1) natural numbers, the sum of their squares, and the geometric-series sum for exponential integrands. Most Exercise 7.8 problems reduce to one of these after you expand f(a+rh).

faq.q: Do I get the same answer as the shortcut antiderivative method?
faq.a: Yes. The limit-of-a-sum value always equals the value from the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Exercise 7.8 makes you do it the long way so you understand where the integral comes from; later exercises let you use antiderivatives.
